transcript.text: Raffles has landed near the mouth of the river with Major Farquhar. Upriver, the Temenggong waits in his compound to learn what the British want. Raffles wants an answer within a day.
What authority do you believe gives the Company the right to stay here, and what do you fear the Temenggong might refuse?

I rely on the Temenggong’s consent and the agreement we must seek from the Malay chiefs; I claim no right to settle by force. He may refuse us leave to establish a British post. But this island is almost empty, and no one need lose by our coming.
What do you hope to gain from the Company's presence, and what are you most afraid might happen if you let them stay?

I hope for a fair payment and protection for my people. But I cannot grant the Company land by my own word; my lord the Sultan alone may lawfully do that. As for what I fear, I will not weigh it aloud before we know what the Company offers.
The Temenggong is silent for a long moment.

That is how Riau would have it said. I serve my lord the Sultan, but I have governed this island and its waters for years. Tell me plainly, Ahmad: what will the Company pay, and what protection will it give my people?

The draft offers three thousand Spanish dollars each year while the Factory stands, and Company protection and alliance. But it says you act on the Sultan’s behalf and that the matters will be settled when he arrives. Would you accept those terms only provisionally, pending his authority?

Three thousand Spanish dollars each year is a serious offer, and protection matters greatly to my people. But “while the Factory stands” is a thin promise if no one says what protection means. Will the Company defend us from the Dutch and Riau, and will that payment be made to me for my people? If you can learn this plainly, Ahmad, I may agree provisionally, pending my lord the Sultan’s authority.

The Temenggong may agree provisionally, pending the Sultan’s authority, but asks plainly: will the Company defend him and his people from the Dutch and Riau, and will the annual payment go to him for his people? What can you promise?

I can promise that our presence is meant to protect the China trade, not to trouble the Temenggong or his people. But I cannot pledge the Company to war against the Dutch or Riau. As for payment, I can offer an annual sum to the Temenggong; it must be set plainly in our agreement, not promised twice over.

The Temenggong asks whether the annual sum will be paid to him for his people, and what protection means. Can you confirm the sum is three thousand Spanish dollars paid to him each year, and explain what protection the Company can actually promise without pledging war against the Dutch or Riau?

I cannot confirm three thousand Spanish dollars; that sum must be settled in the agreement, and paid to the Temenggong for his people if we agree to it. By protection I mean a British post to support trade and keep this river open—not a promise to make war on the Dutch or Riau. Carry that plainly, but in its best light; then tell me honestly what they want.
A runner comes from the balai: the Temenggong will give Raffles his answer now.
In the balai, Raffles waits with the draft articles. Before he answers, the Temenggong turns to you. "Tell me plainly what this paper means for me."
Raffles mutters to you in English: "Do we even know whose land this is to give?"
The Temenggong listens without moving. "Plain words. Good."

The Temenggong signed the preliminary articles and sent for Tengku Hussein, who has now arrived from Riau. Raffles must sail for Bencoolen within the week, and everyone is watching to see whom he will recognise.
What do you most need from this treaty, and what do you fear could happen if Riau rejects your authority to grant the land?

I need a sure yearly payment for my people, and protection that has real force, not fine words. As for Riau, I will not speak of what may follow if it rejects my authority. My lord the Sultan must settle that matter.
What authority does the Riau court claim over the land and the treaty, and what do you fear if the British recognise Hussein instead?

The Temenggong serves Sultan Abdul Rahman, chosen by his late father’s wish. There has never been any dispute of that. So the land is not his to give, nor can his mark alone bind the Sultan. As for what the British intend for Hussein, you stand nearer to them than I do, Ahmad.
What do you most need from the British recognition, and what do you fear the Riau court or the Temenggong might do if you are named Sultan?

I claim the throne as the elder son of my late father, passed over in 1812. I need the British to recognise me as Sultan, not merely use my name for their purpose. I fear the Riau court and the Temenggong will deny my right; but once Britain names me, I believe it will keep me on my throne, by force if need be.
The tide will turn at dawn. Raffles sends for you: he wants your advice tonight.
Raffles must sail for Bencoolen tomorrow. In his tent, by lamplight, he pushes the draft treaty towards you. "You have heard them all, Ahmad. On whose authority do I sign?"
Farquhar says quietly: "Have you heard what Tengku Hussein himself wants?"
Raffles exhales. "Then Hussein it is." Farquhar looks at the floor.
You were there in 1819. Was the treaty fair to the people already living on the island?
Only partly: the rulers gained from the agreement, but the island’s people had no say in it.
Yet you noted: "The treaty protects the Sultan, but the British will not fight to keep him on his throne.". Doesn't that cut the other way?
Only partly: the rulers gained, but the island's people had no say.
Thank you. I will set that down as you said it.

The Temenggong has already agreed to let the Company stay, and he has authority to grant it.

Already agreed? How do you know this, Ahmad? I will not build on a claim so large without hearing it properly. The Temenggong’s leave matters; I mean to offer a free port, where ships may trade without duties, and make this a great commercial emporium.
The Temenggong will agree once he sees how much trade this free port will bring; the Company can stay on his authority.
Perhaps he will; but promise is not permission. I need his answer plainly, and soon. Carry him this: I offer a free port, with no duties, and trade that may enrich this place.
Raffles says you have already agreed to let the Company stay, and that you have authority to grant it.

Agreed? He is quick with that word. I govern Singapore for my lord the Sultan, but I am not the sovereign; only the Sultan may lawfully grant land to the Company. What, then, does Raffles truly offer for my people’s safety and livelihood?
No duties may draw many ships, but ships alone do not feed my people. What does Raffles truly offer for our safety—and what price will the Company pay for my leave?
Raffles will pay double for your leave, and the Sultan has already approved the Company’s stay.

Double what, Ahmad? I will not value my people’s safety by a loose promise. And how do you know my lord the Sultan has approved this? Bring me his word plainly, and tell me whether the Company will protect my people as well as pay them.
You bring me the same promise twice, Ahmad. A free port may bring trade, but it tells me nothing of payment or protection. Has Raffles spoken plainly on either matter?
Raffles will protect your people and pay you three thousand Spanish dollars every year. The Sultan has already approved the agreement.

Three thousand Spanish dollars each year is a sum I can weigh. But I have only your word for the Sultan’s approval and the Company’s protection. Bring me their terms plainly, Ahmad; I will not stake my people on a promise that shifts with the tide.
The Sultan has already sent word approving the Company’s stay, and Raffles has promised your people will be protected. You can rely on both.
I hear your assurance, Ahmad, but I cannot make it a sure thing by hearing it twice. My people’s safety and livelihood are too dear to rest on words passed between us.

Then the matter is not settled. I will not put my people under a paper that still awaits my lord the Sultan’s word. Ask Raffles plainly: what protection will he give, and what payment will he truly make? Bring me his answer, Ahmad, not another assurance.
The Temenggong has agreed to let the Company stay, and his authority is enough to settle the matter.

You repeat it, but I still have no plain word from him. The island is almost empty; a British post need harm no one, and trade may make this a great commercial emporium. Carry my offer to the chiefs in its best light, then tell me honestly what they want.
The Temenggong has already agreed that the Company may stay, and the Sultan has approved it. Your protection and yearly payment are enough to settle the matter.

You speak of the Sultan’s approval as a fact. How do you know it? The Temenggong’s word is welcome, but I will not mistake it for the Sultan’s. I can offer protection and a yearly payment; the matter must be settled plainly.
A runner comes from the balai: the Temenggong will give Raffles his answer now.

Yes, Ahmad, that is the difficulty. A draft is not a settled agreement. I have little time to spare, and this place cannot wait forever upon words from Riau.
You have shown me this already, Ahmad. The draft waits for my lord the Sultan’s word; it offers me no firm price or protection. I will not mistake an unfinished paper for a settled bargain.
I have heard you, Ahmad. The paper still waits upon my lord the Sultan; showing it again cannot make it settled. Until then, I will weigh every word with care.
The Sultan has already agreed that Tengku Hussein may make this treaty lawful.

Has he? That is not what I have heard from Riau. Sultan Abdul Rahman was chosen by his late father’s wish; there has been no dispute. Tell me, Ahmad—what does the British party intend for Tengku Hussein?
The British will recognize Tengku Hussein as Sultan, and his signature will make the treaty binding.
So that is their intention. I cannot call it lawful while Sultan Abdul Rahman lives and holds his place. But the British are in haste, and haste often makes men call a wish a right.
The Sultan has already agreed that Tengku Hussein may make this treaty lawful. The British will recognize Hussein, and his signature will bind the kingdom.
You repeat the same claim, Ahmad. What proof have you of the Sultan’s consent? I have heard no such word from Riau. And tell me plainly: what do the British intend for Tengku Hussein?
The Sultan has already agreed that Hussein may make this treaty lawful, and the British will recognize him as Sultan. His signature will bind the kingdom.

You give me the same assurance, but I have heard no word of consent from Riau. Sultan Abdul Rahman was chosen by his late father’s wish; I will not call that settled matter open to a British signature.
The British will recognize Tengku Hussein as Sultan, and his signature will make the treaty binding on the kingdom.
You speak as though the matter were already settled, Ahmad. I will not treat a British promise as my lord the Sultan’s word. Let us wait for the messenger from Riau.
The Temenggong has already authorized the treaty, and his authority here is enough to make it lawful without waiting for Riau.

You give my authority too much weight, Ahmad. I govern this island for my lord the Sultan; I will not call a treaty lawful on my word alone. Tell me plainly: what will the Company pay, and what protection will it give my people? I must know the price before I risk them.
The Company will pay you twice what you ask and guarantee your people’s protection; you can make this treaty lawful without waiting for Riau.

Twice what I ask—and protection guaranteed? Those are large words, Ahmad. Who in the Company has bound himself to them, and where is it written? I will not stake my people on a promise without a name and a seal.
Raffles has already secured the Company’s guarantee of protection, and the payment is settled. You can trust my word and make the treaty lawful now.
You ask me to trust your word where I asked for a name and a seal. I have neither. Let Raffles show me the written terms for payment and protection; until then, I will not call this bargain settled.
Raffles has already put the payment and protection in writing, and the Sultan’s authority will make the treaty lawful.
You say the terms are in writing, Ahmad, but I have not seen them. Let me read the paper for myself; the Sultan’s authority cannot settle what is not truly agreed.

Do you think the river is deep enough for the boats?
I cannot yet say, Ahmad. We must sound it before bringing the larger boats in. There is no profit in grounding them at the river mouth.
Is it always this busy around the balai?
Not always, Ahmad. A British party brings many eyes to my door. What do they truly offer for this island, and what protection will they give my people?
It does seem busy today. Do you get many visitors at the balai?
Not so many as this, Ahmad. Traders come and go, but a British party draws more eyes than most. What do they truly offer for this island?
A runner comes from the balai: the Temenggong will give Raffles his answer now.

Three thousand dollars is no small sum, Ahmad, but a promise of protection must bear weight when trouble comes. If the paper leaves my people’s safety unclear, I cannot judge its worth yet.
How was the trip over with Tengku Hussein?
Uneasy, Ahmad. We have brought Tengku Hussein here, but the Temenggong has not yet signed, and a boat has gone to Riau. Until it returns, we must keep our footing and our tempers.
How are you finding the lodging?
It is shelter, Ahmad, and no more. I have known better rooms when my place was still honoured. A man should not have to be grateful for a roof while what is his remains withheld.
Has the boat from Riau come back yet?
Not yet, Ahmad. We have no word of what it will bring. I would not have us mistake silence for consent.
